The initiation of lactation coincides with the first exogenous feeding, and newborn pups depend entirely on maternal milk during the initial weeks of life. This weaning mass is particularly critical: females typically reach a wet weight at weaning of 200 grams [Wwx = 200 grams], reflecting the substantial nutrient transfer from the mother during the nursing stage. The period from parturition to dietary transition thus represents a phase of rapid somatic growth, driven by the energetic subsidy of lactation.

The combination of moderate litter size and a compact gestation interval allows females to fit two reproductive events into a single active season.

This sex-based difference in the timing of sexual maturation is common among polygynous or promiscuous rodents.

Longevity records for Sciurus carolinensis indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 23.6 years [am = approximately 23.6 years], though few individuals approach this upper boundary at a temperature of 38.7 °C [T = 38.7 °C]. Senescence in older individuals manifests as reduced tooth wear efficiency and declining body condition during winter months. The physiological death of geriatric squirrels in protected populations occurs through progressive organ failure, marking the completion of a lifespan that balances extended adult survival against a modest reproductive rate.

Seasonal fluctuations in food availability exert a strong influence on body condition and reproductive timing in eastern gray squirrels. Mast crops of oaks and hickories, which constitute the primary dietary resource, vary markedly between years, and females in poor mast years may skip breeding entirely.
